newsitem.title: UK: Local shop owner bids to stop Blair juggernaut.
newsitem.headline: Local shop owner bids to stop Blair juggernaut.

text.p: It crushed John Major's Conservative government at the May 1 election, sweeping six cabinet ministers out of the House of Commons.
But the Tony Blair juggernaut could be stopped in its tracks on Thursday by the owner of a west London furniture store who has never fought a public election in his life.

Polls show John Randall has a fighting chance of denting the "lord-of-all-he-surveys" image of Britain's Labour Prime Minister by winning the first parliamentary by-election of the new parliament for the Conservatives.

Randall is defending a 724-vote majority won by Sir Michael Shersby in Uxbridge, on the western fringes of London, at the May election when Labour swept to power with a record 179-seat majority in parliament.
Labour candidate Andy Slaughter implicitly acknowledges Randall could snatch victory. "We have never thought it would be anything other than close," he told Reuters.
William Hill bookmakers make Slaughter 8-11 favourite and Randall evens to win the contest.

Britain's governing party has not taken a seat from the official opposition at a by-election since 1960. The Conservatives, in power from 1979 to May, last won a parliamentary seat in a by-election in 1989, when their candidate was William Hague, now their new leader.
Before May 1 Uxbridge was seen as solid Conservative territory, with Shersby's majority at the 1992 general election climbing over 12,000.
Shersby's death shortly after the May election triggered Thursday's contest.

Randall parades his local connections proudly -- his store is the biggest in Uxbridge not owned by a national chain, he was Shersby's election agent and his family have lived in the town for generations.
By contrast, Slaughter's candidacy is hampered by what even his aides admit is controversy over his selection.

The Labour general election candidate, David Williams, a local man, did not even make it to the short-list. Instead the nomination went to Slaughter, leader of what to many Uxbridge people is a distant inner London local authority.
Labour's London press officer, Richard Burningham, admits the selection process angered some Labour supporters. One Labour councillor resigned from the party over the issue.
But Burningham described as a "gross exaggeration" reports that 30 local members had refused to work for Slaughter.

"Local Labour supporters appear so ready to let Tony Blair take us all for mugs," one resident wrote to the local paper. "If he thinks we are all going to troop into the polling booths like lambs to the Slaughter...he's got another think coming."
Randall said support in the constituency for the two main parties had changed little since the May election.
But he said: "I have had people come up to me and say I am a Labour Party member, but I am going to vote for you'."
"I don't suppose they would ever vote for me again, but they want a local man to represent them, not an outsider."

A Conservative victory, however narrow, would be an encouraging start for Hague, elected to replace Major as Conservative leader last month, perhaps signalling the beginning of what would be a long, hard road back to power.
The result of the by-election is expected in the early hours of Friday.
